body:
What Makes a Fuel a Biofuel?

A biofuel is a fuel produced from biological material. The term includes gaseous fuels such as biogas, but it is commonly used in transport-energy discussions for liquid biofuels, particularly ethanol and biodiesel.

Ethanol and biodiesel are not interchangeable. They are different substances, produced through different processes and ordinarily blended with different conventional fuels.

Bioethanol

Bioethanol is ethyl alcohol produced from suitable biological feedstocks. Sugars can be fermented by microorganisms, commonly yeast such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae, to produce ethanol and carbon dioxide.

Sugarcane juice and sugar-rich materials provide fermentable sugars. Starch-rich materials, such as suitable grains, first require conversion of starch into sugars before fermentation. The resulting ethanol is purified for its intended use.

In petrol blending, E20 denotes fuel containing approximately 20% ethanol and 80% petrol by volume. The number refers to the blend composition, not the percentage reduction in greenhouse-gas emissions or the percentage of total transport energy supplied by ethanol.

Biodiesel

Biodiesel is commonly produced from vegetable oils, used cooking oils or suitable animal fats through a chemical reaction called transesterification. The process produces fatty acid esters, usually fatty acid methyl esters when methanol is used, and glycerol as a coproduct.

Biodiesel is ordinarily blended with conventional diesel. For example, B20 denotes approximately 20% biodiesel and 80% conventional diesel by volume.

Modern renewable diesel produced by hydrogen-based processing of biological oils or fats is chemically different from conventional ester-based biodiesel, even though both can originate from biological feedstocks.

FeatureBioethanolBiodiesel
Main substanceEthyl alcoholFatty acid esters
Typical feedstockSugars, starches or processed celluloseVegetable oils and suitable fats
Principal conversionFermentation of sugarsTransesterification
Usual fossil-fuel blendPetrolDiesel
ExampleE20B20

First-Generation and Advanced Biofuels

Biofuels are often classified according to the feedstock and production pathway. These categories are useful, but their boundaries are not identical in every policy or technical publication.

  • First-generation biofuels: Commonly produced from food-related sugars, starches or vegetable oils, such as ethanol from sugarcane juice or starch-rich grain.
  • Second-generation biofuels: Commonly use non-food lignocellulosic feedstocks such as agricultural straw, suitable forestry residues or sugarcane bagasse. Producing ethanol from these materials involves breaking down their complex structural carbohydrates into fermentable sugars.
  • Third-generation biofuels: Often associated with algae-based feedstocks. Many such pathways remain at research, pilot or limited commercial stages.

The generation label does not change the identity of the final fuel. Ethanol produced from sugarcane juice and ethanol produced from processed agricultural straw are chemically ethanol; the distinction concerns feedstock and production pathway.

India's Biofuel Programmes and Their Status

India's Ethanol Blended Petrol Programme promotes the blending of ethanol with petrol. The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas dashboard reported 20.00% ethanol blending for the stated ethanol supply year data period of November 2025 to June 2026. This is a reported blending figure for that period; it does not establish that every individual petrol sale contained exactly 20% ethanol.

The Pradhan Mantri JI-VAN Yojana, notified in 2019, supports advanced biofuel projects. A Union Cabinet decision announced on 9 August 2024 extended its implementation period to 2028–29 and broadened the eligible advanced biofuel feedstocks and approaches. The policy particularly connects agricultural and forestry residues with advanced biofuel production.

Prelims focus

  • Ethanol is produced by fermenting sugars; Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a commonly used yeast.
  • Biodiesel is commonly made through transesterification of oils or fats.
  • E20 refers to approximately 20% ethanol by volume in petrol; B20 refers to 20% biodiesel in diesel.
  • Second-generation ethanol can be made from suitable lignocellulosic residues.
  • India's petroleum ministry dashboard reported 20.00% ethanol blending for November 2025–June 2026.
  • Trap: First-generation and second-generation ethanol differ in feedstock and processing, not in the chemical identity of ethanol.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, chapter 'Microbes in Human Welfare', section 10.2.1, 'Fermented Beverages'; Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, 'Ethanol Blending' dashboard, data period November 2025–June 2026, accessed 16 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, 'Cabinet approves Amendment in Pradhan Mantri JI-VAN Yojana', 9 August 2024; International Energy Agency, 'Biofuels', accessed 16 November 2026.]

title: Liquid Biofuels: Bioethanol, Biodiesel and Fuel Generations

body:
Why Renewable Biomass Is Not Automatically Carbon-Neutral

When biomass is burned, carbon dioxide enters the atmosphere. Plants may subsequently remove carbon dioxide through photosynthesis as they grow. This is the basis for describing biomass as part of a relatively short biological carbon cycle.

However, it does not follow that every biomass fuel has zero net greenhouse-gas emissions. Growing, collecting, transporting and processing the feedstock can release additional greenhouse gases. Changes in land use can also release carbon stored in vegetation and soils.

Lifecycle assessment evaluates environmental impacts across the stages of a product or energy pathway, rather than considering only its final use. For biofuels, the stages can include feedstock cultivation or collection, processing, transport and fuel use, together with relevant land-use changes.

Important Sources of Lifecycle Emissions

  • Land preparation and cultivation: Machinery and agricultural inputs may require fossil energy.
  • Fertiliser use: Agricultural soils can release nitrous oxide, a powerful greenhouse gas.
  • Processing: Heat, electricity and chemical inputs used to manufacture fuels may cause emissions.
  • Transport: Feedstocks and finished fuels must often be moved between farms, factories and users.
  • Combustion: Burning biofuels releases carbon dioxide, even if part of that carbon was recently absorbed during plant growth.
  • Land-use change: Converting forests, grasslands or other carbon-rich ecosystems into energy-crop production can release stored carbon and harm biodiversity.
  • Methane leakage: Escaped methane from biogas systems can substantially reduce their greenhouse-gas advantage.

Direct and Indirect Land-Use Change

Direct land-use change occurs when land is explicitly converted for producing biofuel feedstock, such as clearing a forest to establish a plantation.

Indirect land-use change can occur when existing food or feed production is displaced to another area, contributing to the conversion of land elsewhere. These indirect effects are difficult to measure precisely, but they can materially affect the assessment of a biofuel's climate impact.

Consequently, a fuel cannot be judged solely by whether its starting material came from a plant.

Food, Land and Water Trade-Offs

Food-related crops used for fuel production may compete with food and feed markets for agricultural land, irrigation water and other inputs. The scale of competition varies with the crop, location, agricultural practices and availability of genuinely surplus material.

Waste-based pathways can reduce direct competition for food-producing land, but only when the feedstock is sustainably collected. Removing excessive straw from agricultural land, for example, may reduce soil organic matter and increase erosion. Used cooking oil may avoid the need for new oil crops, but its collection and processing must still be managed responsibly.

Air Pollution Is Different from Greenhouse-Gas Emissions

Burning biomass can release particulate matter, carbon monoxide and other air pollutants, particularly where combustion is incomplete or pollution-control measures are inadequate. These pollutants affect local air quality and health.

Greenhouse-gas emissions are assessed for their contribution to climate change. A fuel pathway may have a lower lifecycle greenhouse-gas impact than a fossil-fuel alternative while still requiring careful control of local air pollution.

Conditions for a Better Environmental Outcome

The most favourable bioenergy applications generally use suitable residues or wastes without undermining other important uses, avoid conversion of high-carbon ecosystems, control methane and air-pollutant emissions, and return nutrients to soil where appropriate. They also minimise unnecessary processing and transport energy.

Carbon neutrality is a conclusion to be demonstrated, not a property guaranteed by the word biomass. The result depends on feedstock origin, land-use effects, processing energy, emissions control and the period over which carbon is absorbed and released.

Prelims focus

  • Lifecycle emissions include production, processing, transport and use, with relevant land-use changes.
  • Fertiliser use can contribute nitrous oxide emissions.
  • Biogas methane leakage weakens its climate benefit.
  • Direct land-use change occurs at the feedstock-production site; indirect land-use change may occur elsewhere through displaced production.
  • Excessive crop-residue removal can harm soil fertility and conservation.
  • Trap: A renewable biofuel does not necessarily have zero emissions or zero air-pollution impacts.

[Sources: International Energy Agency, 'Carbon Accounting for Sustainable Biofuels', published 23 July 2024, overview and discussion of lifecycle emissions and land-use change; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, chapter 'Environment and Sustainable Development', section on environmental carrying capacity; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 'How Does Anaerobic Digestion Work?', accessed 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The biological carbon cycle sits within a wider lifecycle assessment that also counts cultivation, fossil energy, land-use change and biogas methane leakage.
pictures.caption: Biofuel emissions must be assessed across the entire production and use cycle.

title: Environmental Sustainability of Biomass and Biofuels

body:
Origin of Geothermal Energy

Geothermal energy is energy obtained from the Earth's internal heat. Temperature generally increases with depth beneath the surface. This rise is described by the geothermal gradient, although the rate of increase varies with geological conditions.

Heat inside the Earth comes partly from naturally occurring radioactive decay and partly from heat remaining from Earth's formation. In some regions, geothermal heat reaches shallow depths because of geological structures, tectonic activity or hot rock formations.

Underground water may absorb this heat. Where suitable pathways exist, hot water or steam may reach the surface as hot springs or other geothermal features. However, a hot spring does not by itself establish that a site is suitable for electricity generation.

Essential Conditions for Conventional Geothermal Power

Conventional geothermal electricity production generally depends on 3 important resource conditions:

  • Heat: Underground rock and fluid must be sufficiently hot for the intended application.
  • Fluid: Water or another fluid must be available to carry heat from the underground resource.
  • Permeability: The rocks need connected spaces or fractures through which fluid can circulate.

Geological exploration therefore considers more than temperature. A deeply buried hot rock formation may contain substantial heat but still be difficult to use if sufficient fluid or connected pathways are unavailable.

Direct Heat Use and Electricity Generation

Geothermal heat can be used directly for bathing, space heating, greenhouses, drying and suitable industrial processes. These applications do not necessarily require temperatures high enough for electricity generation.

Electricity generation uses underground heat to produce vapour that drives a turbine and generator. The method depends largely on the available temperature and the form of the geothermal fluid.

TechnologyWorking principleResource suitability
Dry-steam plantUses naturally occurring underground steam to drive a turbineSteam-dominated geothermal reservoir
Flash-steam plantPressure reduction causes sufficiently hot geothermal water to form steamHigh-temperature hot-water reservoir
Binary-cycle plantTransfers geothermal heat to a separate low-boiling working fluidCan use relatively moderate-temperature geothermal resources

In a binary-cycle plant, the underground geothermal fluid and the separate working fluid normally remain in different circuits. Heat passes between them through a heat exchanger. This arrangement helps explain why binary plants can use some resources that are not hot enough for conventional flash-steam generation.

Geothermal Heat Pumps Are Another Application

A ground-source heat pump transfers heat between a building and the relatively stable temperature of the shallow ground. It can provide heating or cooling by using electricity to move heat. This is different from a geothermal power plant that extracts high-temperature underground heat to generate electricity.

Availability and Limitations

Suitable geothermal resources can provide relatively steady energy throughout the day and night, unlike the daily variations of solar energy. Nevertheless, the local reservoir must be managed carefully. Excessive extraction or inadequate reinjection can reduce reservoir pressure or temperature and affect long-term performance.

Other important constraints include drilling difficulty, mineral-rich fluids, possible hydrogen sulphide release and the need to protect groundwater. Site selection and responsible operation are essential.

Prelims focus

  • Geothermal energy uses the Earth's internal heat.
  • Conventional geothermal power generally requires sufficient heat, fluid and permeability.
  • Dry-steam plants use underground steam directly.
  • Flash-steam plants obtain steam by reducing the pressure of very hot geothermal water.
  • Binary-cycle plants transfer heat to a separate low-boiling working fluid.
  • Trap: A geothermal heat pump provides heating or cooling; it is not the same as a geothermal electricity-generating plant.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter 'Mineral and Power Resources', printed pp. 35–36; U.S. Department of Energy, 'Geothermal Basics' and 'Geothermal Electricity Generation', sections on resource conditions and electricity generation, accessed 16 November 2026.]

title: Geothermal Energy: Earth's Heat, Resource Conditions and Power Technologies
